# Port Notice PORT-N-07/2026 — Monsoon working restrictions: West Basin and outer anchorage

> Demo-world instrument of the Mundra Port Operations Portal, reproduced in the
> Sagar Drishti knowledge library. This is a fictional demo document and not a
> publication of any real port authority.

Ref No: PORT-N-07/2026 · Type: NOTICE · Category: Port operations · Status: IN FORCE
Issued by: Harbour Master, Mundra (Capt. Rajiv Nair) · Issued: 15 June 2026 · Effective: 25 June 2026
Acknowledgement required: YES (all shipping agents and terminal operators)
Tags: monsoon, UKC, bunkering, West Basin, anchorage

Register summary (verbatim): "Cape vessels to maintain 20% additional UKC at WB
berths during SW monsoon; bunkering suspended at outer anchorage above sea
state 5."

## Text of the notice (as issued)

"During the South-West monsoon period, all capesize vessels berthing at
WB-1/WB-2 shall maintain an additional 20% under-keel clearance over the
declared minimum. Bunker barge operations at the outer anchorage stand
suspended whenever sea state exceeds 5 or wind exceeds 25 knots sustained.
Masters shall confirm compliance on the pre-arrival checklist."

## 1. Applicability and duration

1.1 This notice applies within Mundra port limits for the declared South-West
monsoon period. The Harbour Master declares the opening and closing of the
monsoon period by message to all agents; it ordinarily runs from June to the
end of September.

1.2 The under-keel clearance (UKC) provision applies to capesize dry bulk
vessels working the West Basin berths WB-1 and WB-2 (West Basin Coal Termin

end of September.

1.2 The under-keel clearance (UKC) provision applies to capesize dry bulk
vessels working the West Basin berths WB-1 and WB-2 (West Basin Coal Terminal).
The bunkering provision applies to all bunker barge operations at the outer
anchorage, irrespective of vessel type.

## 2. Under-keel clearance at WB-1 / WB-2

2.1 The declared minimum UKC for the West Basin remains as promulgated in the
port's standing navigational data. During the monsoon period, capesize vessels
shall plan arrival drafts, tidal windows and ballast conditions so that the UKC
actually available alongside and in the approach is not less than 120% of that
declared minimum (that is, the declared minimum plus a further 20%).

2.2 Pilots will verify the computed UKC on the master–pilot exchange. Where the
20% additional margin cannot be demonstrated for the intended tidal window, the
movement will be rescheduled to a suitable tide or the vessel will be lightened
at anchorage as arranged by the agent.

2.3 Swell allowance: the additional margin accounts for monsoon swell response
(heave, pitch and squat at low speed). It is not to be traded against squat
calculations; the 20% is applied after squat and swell response are deducted.

## 3. Bunkering at the outer anchorage

3.1 Bunker barge operations at the outer anchorage stand suspended whenever
either of the following is observed or forecast for the operation window:
(a) sea state exceeding 5 on the WMO scale; or
(b) sustained wind exceeding 25 knots.

3.2 Marine Control is the deciding authority on prevailing

Barges already alongside a receiving vessel when a suspension is declared shall

3.3 Licensed bunker suppliers (see the port licence register — e.g. Saurashtra

## 4. Mooring and berth safety during the monsoon

4.1 The pre-monsoon mooring standard for cape vessels at the West Basin is
raised for the duration of this notice: masters shall run additional lines as
directed by the pilot or berthing master, and shall keep winch brakes tested
and rendered to the correct settings.

4.2 A tug may be held on standby at the Harbour Master's discretion during
squall passage. Costs follow the schedule of marine charges.

## 5. Pre-arrival confirmation

5.1 Masters shall confirm compliance with this notice on the pre-arrival
checklist submitted through the agent with the vessel's pre-arrival
notification. Calls that cannot confirm the UKC margin will be scheduled
accordingly.

("Anchorage allocation policy — priority matrix", issued by the Harbo

# Circular CIRC-07/2024 — Container VGM verification procedure at the gate

> Demo-world instrument of the Mundra Port Operations Portal, reproduced in the
> Sagar Drishti knowledge library. This is a fictional demo document and not a
> publication of any real port authority.

Ref No: CIRC-07/2024 · Type: CIRCULAR · Category: Port operations · Status: IN FORCE
Issued by: Port Operations, Mundra · Issued: 18 March 2024 · Effective: 1 April 2024
Acknowledgement required: YES (shipping agents, CHAs, terminal operators)
Tags: SOLAS, VGM, container, gate, weighbridge

Register summary (verbatim): "Verified Gross Mass to be declared and weighed at
the terminal gate for all export containers per SOLAS Ch VI reg 2."

## Text of the circular (as issued)

"Shipping agents and CHAs shall submit VGM via Method 1 (weighing the packed
container) at the terminal gate weighbridge; Method 2 (calculated) declarations
must carry the shipper's certified weighing procedure on file. Containers
without a VGM record on file will not be permitted to load."

## 1. Background

1.1 SOLAS Chapter VI, regulation 2 requires the shipper to provide the Verified
Gross Mass (VGM) of a packed export container before it may be loaded on board.
Two methods are recognised internationally: Method 1 — weighing the packed and
sealed container; Method 2 — weighing all packages, dunnage and securing
material and adding the container tare, under a certified procedure.

1.2 This circular standardises how VGM is captured at the container terminals
(MICT, AMCT, AMC2, CT-3, CT-4) so that the planning systems hold a single

title: Circular CIRC-07/2024 — Container VGM verification procedure at the gate
source: Mundra Port Operations Portal — instrument register (Sagar Drishti demo world)
text:
he container tare, under a certified procedure.

1.2 This circular standardises how VGM is captured at the container terminals
(MICT, AMCT, AMC2, CT-3, CT-4) so that the planning systems hold a single
authoritative VGM per container.

## 2. Procedure at the gate

2.1 Method 1 (default): every export container passes the terminal gate
weighbridge on entry. The weighbridge reading, less the certified tare of the
road vehicle, is recorded as the VGM against the container number and shipper,
and flows automatically to the terminal operating system and the load planner.

2.2 Method 2 (by exception): a shipper approved for Method 2 lodges the
calculated VGM in the pre-advice. The approval requires the shipper's certified
weighing procedure to be on file with the terminal and referenced in each
declaration. Method 2 boxes may still be check-weighed at the gate.

2.3 Discrepancy handling: where the gate weight differs from a declared VGM by
more than the permitted tolerance of ±5% or 500 kg (whichever is less), the
gate weight prevails, the pre-advice is flagged for the shipper's account, and
repeated discrepancies are reported to the line and to the licensing desk.

## 3. No VGM — no load

3.1 A container without an accepted VGM record on file will not be permitted to
load. It will be held in a designated yard block at the shipper's cost until
the VGM is established by weighing.

3.2 Terminal planners shall not accept manual overrides of the VGM field;
corrections flow only through a revised weighment or a revised Method 2
declaration.

Ref No: PORT-N-02/2023 · Type: NOTICE · Category: Port operations · Status: WITHDRAWN
Issued by: Harbour Master, Mundra · Issued: 12 June 2023 · Effective: 13 June 2023
Acknowledgement required: No
Tags: cyclone, contingency, weather, evacuation

Register summary (verbatim): "Precautionary berthing suspension and vessel
evacuation to sea ahead of Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Biparjoy making landfall
near Jakhau, Kutch."

## Text of the notice (as issued)

"Following IMD tracking of Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Biparjoy, all vessels
alongside shall complete cargo operations and vacate berths by 1800 hrs on
14 June 2023, proceeding to open sea or a designated safe anchorage. Port
operations will remain suspended until an all-clear survey of berths, cranes
and navigational aids is completed after landfall."

## 1. Sequence ordered by this notice (June 2023)

1.1 On issue (12 June): no fresh berthing; vessels at anchorage held pending
the storm track; agents advised masters to keep engines on notice.

1.2 By 1800 hrs, 14 June: all vessels alongside to have completed or secured
cargo operations, disconnected shore connections, and vacated berths under
pil

1.2 By 1800 hrs, 14 June: all vessels alongside to have completed or secured
cargo operations, disconnected shore connections, and vacated berths under

1.3 During passage of the storm: port closed to all movements; tugs and craft

1.4 After landfall: resumption only on the Harbour Master's all-clear,

local navigational warnings.

2.1 The notice was withdrawn after the post-storm all-clear survey was
completed and normal operations resumed. It remains on the register as a
WITHDRAWN instrument and is retained in this library as the pattern for
cyclone-season contingency action.

- Early, time-bound evacuation to sea protects both ships and berth structures;

  aids to navigation) is now the standard resumption checklist an

Portal instrument register entry — Ref No MSA-1958, type ACT, status IN FORCE,
issued by the Parliament of India (assented 30 October 1958, brought into force
from 1960). Register summary (verbatim): "Principal Indian statute governing
merchant shipping — registration, certification, safety, crew and liability."

## What the Act is

The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is India's principal merchant shipping
statute. It consolidates the law on ships, seafarers and shipowners, gives
effect in Indian law to the major IMO and ILO instruments India has ratified,
and is administered by the Directorate General of Shipping (DG Shipping) under
the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. It has been amended many times
(notably to absorb SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and MLC obligations), and detailed
requirements sit in rules made under it — for example the Merchant Shipping
(STCW) Rules, 2014.

- Administration: establishes the National Shipping Board and the shipping

  Departments, surveyors, shipping masters and seamen's welfare machinery.

## What the Act is

The Major Port Authorities Act, 2021 replaced the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963
as the governing statute for India's major ports — the ports administered by
the Union government (for example Deendayal Port at Kandla, Jawaharlal Nehru
Port, Mumbai, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Cochin and the other centrally
administered ports). Its stated purpose is to give major ports more autonomy
and professional, board-style governance.

## Key features in plain language

- Board of Major Port Authority: each major port is run by a compact statutory
  Board (chairperson, deputy chairperson, government and stakeholder members,
  including a labour representative) in place of the older, larger port trust.
- Greater autonomy: the Board can make its own master plan for the port area,
  enter contracts, create posts, and raise loans within limits — decisions that
  previously needed central approval in many cases.
- Tariff liberalisation: Boards (and PPP concessionaires under their
  concessions) frame their own scale of rates; the former role of the Tariff
  Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) as tariff-setter was ended, with TAMP-era
  functions folded into the new scheme.
- Adjudicatory Board: an Adjudicatory Board handles specified disputes —
  notably between ports and PPP concessionaires — and residu

  functions folded into the new scheme.
- Adjudicatory Board: an Adjudicatory Board handles specified disputes —
  notably between ports and PPP concessionaires — and residual TAMP work.
- Public-private partnership: the Act explicitly contemplates concession
  agreements for berths and terminals, which is how most modern container

- CSR and development: Boards may spend on corporate social responsibility and

The Act applies only to the notified major ports. Mundra is a non-major port
in Gujarat: it is regulated under the Indian Ports Act, 1908 read with Gujarat
state law and the Gujarat Maritime Board's oversight, and is operated by a
private developer. So in the Sagar Drishti demo world, the Major Port
Authorities Act is background law — useful for benchmarking against major-port
practice (tariff structures, concession models, port authority boards) — while
the port's own conservancy powers flow from the 1908 Act framework.

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 overview.

## What the Act is

The Indian Ports Act, 1908 is the century-old framework statute for the safety
and conservancy of ports in India. Where the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021
governs who runs a major port, the 1908 Act supplies the basic port-police
powers that apply at ports generally — including the non-major ports
administered by state governments and state maritime boards. Mundra, as a
Gujarat non-major port, sits under this framework read with Gujarat state law
(the Gujarat Maritime Board regime).

## Core concepts in plain language

- Declared ports and port limits: government notifies which places are ports
  under the Act and fixes their port limits — the water and foreshore within
  which the Act's rules bite.
- Port rules: the government may make rules for a port on practically every
  operational subject — regulating vessel traffic and berthing, anchoring
  stations, speed, use of tugs and moorings, ballast and cargo handling,
  keeping fairways clear, fire precautions, and the time and manner of
  entering or leaving.
- Conservator of the port: every port has a conservator (at Mundra the
  demo-world office of the Harbour Master, with a Deputy Conservator in the
  role directory) who exercises the day-to-day powers: directing where a
  vessel berths or anchors, ordering a vessel to be moved, boarding and

- Safety and conservancy: prohibitions with penalties on throwing ballast or
  rubbish into port waters, damaging buoys and beacons, careless navigation,

- Port dues and fees: the legal basis for levying port dues on vessels

# SOLAS 1974 — chapters overview

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo

Portal instrument register entry — Ref No SOLAS-74, type CONVENTION, status IN
FORCE, issued by the IMO (adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980).
Register summary (verbatim): "Core IMO convention on ship safety —
construction, fire protection, life-saving, radio, navigation."

## What SOLAS is

The International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), 1974, as
amended, is the central IMO treaty on ship safety. It applies broadly to ships
on international voyages, sets minimum standards for construction, equipment
and operation, and is kept current through the tacit-amendment procedure, so
its chapters evolve continuously. Flag states certify compliance; port states
verify it through PSC inspections.

## The chapters in plain language

- Chapter I — General provisions: application, surveys and the certificates a
  ship must carry (and which PSC officers check first).
- Chapter II-1 — Construction: subdivision and damage stability, machinery and
  electrical installations.
- Chapter II-2 — Fire protection, fire detection and fire extinction: the fire
  safety regime, with the FSS Code alongside.
- Chapter III — Life-saving appliances and arrangements: lifeboats, liferafts,
  lifejackets, drills — with the LSA Code.
- Chapter IV — Radiocommunications: the GMDSS distress and safety
  communication

# MARPOL 73/78 — Annexes I–VI overview

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo

Portal instrument register entry — Ref No MARPOL-73/78, type CONVENTION,

2 October 1983). Register summary (verbatim): "Annexes I–VI: oil, chemicals,
packaged goods, sewage, garbage and air emissions from ships."

## What MARPOL is

The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships
(MARPOL) is the main IMO treaty on preventing operational and accidental
pollution from ships. It works through six technical annexes, each with its own
discharge standards, equipment and survey requirements, record books, and — for
several annexes — an obligation on ports to provide adequate reception
facilities for the wastes ships cannot discharge at sea.

## The annexes in plain language

- Annex I — Oil: controls discharge of oil and oily mixtures from machinery
  spaces and cargo areas of tankers; requires oil filtering equipment, the Oil
  Record Book, IOPP certificate, double hulls for tankers, and the shipboard
  oil pollution emergency plan (SOPEP). Port link: sludge and bilge landings,
  and the Tier-1 spill response SOP in this library.
- Annex II — Noxious liquid substances in bulk: categorises chemical cargoes
  (X, Y, Z) and sets stripping, prewash and discharge rules for chemical
  tanker operations, with the C

  tanker operations, with the Cargo Record Book.
- Annex III — Harmful substances carried by sea in packaged form: packaging,
  marking, labelling and documentation rules for marine pollutants inside the
  IMDG framework.
- Annex IV — Sewage: discharge standards and holding/treatment plant
  requirements; untreated sewage stays out of nearshore waters, hence sewage
  landings or treated discharge only.
- Annex V — Garbage: the "nothing overboard by default" annex. Discharge of
  garbage at sea is generally prohibited (plastics absolutely), with narrow

# ISPS Code — security levels and roles overview

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo

## What the ISPS Code is

The International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code is the maritime
security regime adopted after 2001 and made mandatory through SOLAS Chapter
XI-2 (in force July 2004). It applies to ships on international voyages
(passenger ships, cargo ships of 500 GT and over, MODUs) and to the port
facilities serving them. Part A of the Code is mandatory; Part B is guidance.
Each government designates the authorities that approve security assessments
and plans (in India, the Directorate General of Shipping is the designated
authority for the ISPS framework).

## The three security levels

- Security Level 1 — normal: the level at which ships and port facilities
  routinely operate; minimum protective measures are maintained at all times
  (access control, identity checks, monitoring of restricted areas). Commonly
  spoken of as "MARSEC Level 1", the usage the Mundra demo portal follows.
- Security Level 2 — heightened: a raised risk of a security incident;
  additional protective measures are applied for as long as the risk persists
  (more thorough checks, escorting, tighter access).
- Security Level 3 — exceptional: an incident is probable or imminent; further
  specific measures apply for a limited period, in close liaison with security
  agencies. Level 3 is se

tighter access).
- Security Level 3 — exceptional: an incident is probable or imminent; further
  specific measures apply for a limited period, in close liaison with security
  agencies. Level 3 is set by the government, not by the facility.

Ships must respond to the level set by the port facility or coastal state
(and may never operate below their flag's set level). A ship may request a
Declaration of Security (DoS) — a signed agreement between ship and facility
on who does which security duty during the interface.

## The key roles

- CSO — Company Security Officer: the company's designated person for ship
  security assessments, plans and audits across the fleet.
- SSO — Ship Security Officer: the officer on board responsible for the Ship
  Security Plan (SSP), drills and liaison with the facility.
- PFSO — Port Facility Security Officer: responsible for the Port Facility
  Security Assessment (PFSA) and Port Facility Security Plan (PFSP), for
  setting local measures at each level, and for coordination with ships (the
  office that issues security advisories such as ISPS-ADV-02/2026 in the
  Mundra demo portal).
- RSO — Recognised Security Organisation: may perform assessments or verify
  plans where the government permits.

## Documents and verification

Ships carry an International Ship Security Certificate (ISSC) after
verification of the approved SSP; they maintain security records and a ship
security alert system (SSAS). Port facilities keep the approved PFSP current
and exercise it. PSC officers may check the ISSC and basic security measures;
control measures for

# Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 — titles overview

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo
> library. This is a plain-language overview in the library's own words, not
> convention text; consult the ILO's consolidated MLC, 2006 for legal use.

## What the MLC is

The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 (MLC, 2006) is the ILO's consolidated
"seafarers' bill of rights" — it gathers dozens of older maritime labour
instruments into one convention covering nearly every aspect of a seafarer's
working and living conditions. It entered into force in 2013; India ratified
it in 2015 and implements it through the Merchant Shipping Act framework and
rules. The convention pairs each Regulation with a mandatory Standard (Part A)
and guidance (Part B), organised under five Titles.

## The five Titles in plain language

- Title 1 — Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship: minimum age
  (16, with night-work and hazardous-work protections under 18), medical
  fitness certification (a seafarer medical certificate is valid at most two
  years), training and qualifications, and regulation of recruitment and
  placement services (manning agents must be licensed and may not charge the
  seafarer for placement).
- Title 2 — Conditions of employment: a signed seafarer's employment agreement
  (SEA), wages paid at least monthly with allotments, hours of work and rest
  (maximum hours of work or minimum hours of rest limits), paid annual leave,
  repatriation at the shipowner's cost, compensation for ship loss, manning
  levels, and career development.

- Title 3 — Accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering: cabin
  and mess standards on new ships, recreational facilities, and food — free of

- Title 4 — Health protection, medical care, welfare and social security

- Title 5 — Compliance and enforcement: flag state inspection and — for ships

# STCW certification structure and the Merchant Shipping (STCW) Rules, 2014

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo
> library. This is a plain-language overview in the library's own words, not
> the text of the convention or rules; consult the STCW Convention/Code and the
> gazetted Indian rules for legal use.

Portal instrument register entry — Ref No MS-STCW-2014, type RULES, status IN
FORCE, issued by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (20 June 2014).
Register summary (verbatim): "Indian implementation of STCW 2010 (Manila
amendments) — competency, certification and watchkeeping."

## What STCW is

The International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and
Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW), 1978, with its 1995 overhaul and the 2010
Manila amendments, sets the global minimum standards a seafarer must meet to
serve in a given capacity. The STCW Code's Part A holds the mandatory
competence tables; Part B is guidance. Certificates issued by one party are
recognised by others through endorsement, which is what makes crews
internationally employable.

## Structure of the convention chapters

- Chapter I — General provisions: definitions, certificate format,
  revalidation (certificates of competency are revalidated at intervals not
  exceeding five years), medical standards (medical certificates valid at most
  two years), quality systems, and fraud prevention.
- Chapter II — Master and deck department: officer in charge of a
  navigational watch, chief mate and master, with tonnage bands.
- Chapter III — Engine dep

s), quality systems, and fraud prevention.
- Chapter II — Master and deck department: officer in charge of a
  navigational watch, chief mate and master, with tonnage bands.
- Chapter III — Engine department: officer in charge of an engineering watch,
  second engineer and chief engineer, with power bands; electro-technical
  officer (ETO) certification came in with Manila 2010.
- Chapter IV — Radiocommunication operators: GMDSS operator certification
  (the GOC most deck officers hold).
- Chapter V — Special training: additional certification for tanker personnel
  (oil, chemical, gas), and special-ship training (e.g. passenger ships; polar
  and IGF training were added later).
- Chapter VI — Emergency, occupational safety, security and survival:
  the certificates of proficiency everyone at sea holds — Basic Safety
  Training (personal survival, fire prevention/fighting, elementary first
  aid, personal safety and social responsibility), survival craft (PSCRB),
  advanced fire fighting, medical first aid/care, and security training.
- Chapter VII — Alternative certification: functional certification pathways.
- Chapter VIII — Watchkeeping: fitness for duty and rest hours (minimum 10
  hours of rest in 24, 77 in 7 days, alignable with MLC), watch arrangements
  and principles to be observed.

## Certificate types in practice

- CoC — Certificate of Competency: the licence to serve as officer at a given
  level (e.g. Master FG; MEO Class 1/2 on the engine side in Indian usage).
- CoP — Certificate of Proficiency: task/skill certificates (BST, AFF, PSCRB,
  tanker endorsemen

source: Sagar Drishti demo library — reference summary compiled from public sources
text:
erve as officer at a given
  level (e.g. Master FG; MEO Class 1/2 on the engine side in Indian usage).
- CoP — Certificate of Proficiency: task/skill certificates (BST, AFF, PSCRB,
  tanker endorsements, security awareness/designated duties).
- Endorsements: the flag's recognition attesting a CoC for service on its
  ships; watchkeeping ratings and able-seafarer grades are certified too.

## The Indian rules of 2014

The Merchant Shipping (Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping)
Rules, 2014 carry the Manila-amended convention into Indian law under the
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. DG Shipping is the administration: it approves
maritime training institutes, conducts/oversees examinations, issues CoCs,
CoPs and endorsements, maintains the INDoS seafarer identity database, and
issues the Continuous Discharge Certificate (CDC) that records sea service.
In the Mundra demo world, seafarer records show exactly this document set —
CDC number, INDoS number, CoC grade, GMDSS GOC, medical fitness (two-year
validity) and STCW safety certificates — issued by "DG Shipping, India".

## Port relevance

Crew certificate checks during port state control and flag inspections,
crewing-desk verification before sign-on, rest-hour compliance in casualty
investigations, and the currency alerts the demo portal raises when a
certificate (say a medical or BST) is expiring or expired.

# Port State Control — Indian Ocean MoU inspection regime overview

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo

## What port state control is

Port State Control (PSC) is the inspection of foreign-flag ships in national
ports to verify that the ship and its crew comply with the international
conventions — SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, MLC, Load Lines, ISPS and the rest — and to
detain substandard ships until serious deficiencies are put right. PSC is the
safety net behind flag state certification.

## The Indian Ocean MoU

Port states coordinate regionally through Memoranda of Understanding. India is
a member of the Indian Ocean Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control
(IOMOU), established in 1998, whose secretariat is hosted in Goa, India. Around
twenty maritime authorities of the Indian Ocean rim participate. The MoU
harmonises inspection procedures (aligned with IMO's PSC procedures
resolution), sets a regional inspection effort, runs an annual report and a
central inspection database, and conducts Concentrated Inspection Campaigns
(CICs) on chosen topics jointly with other regions. In India, PSC is exercised
by DG Shipping's Mercantile Marine Department surveyors at the ports.

## How an inspection runs

1. Selection: ships are targeted by risk — factors include ship type and age,
   flag performance, company performance, and the time since and outcome of
   the last inspection in the

inspection runs

1. Selection: ships are targeted by risk — factors include ship type and age,
   flag performance, company performance, and the time since and outcome of
   the last inspection in the region.
2. Initial inspection: certificates and documents, overall condition, crew
   certification and manning, and a walk-through of decks, bridge, engine room
   and accommodation.
3. Clear grounds → more detailed inspection: if certificates are invalid or
   the surveyor forms clear grounds that the ship does not substantially meet
   convention standards, the inspection deepens (operational drills, opening
   up systems).
4. Deficiencies and action: each deficiency is recorded on Form B with a code.
5. Detention: where deficiencies are clearly hazardous to safety, health or
   the environment, the ship is detained until rectification; detentions are
   published by the MoU.

## Deficiency and action coding in plain language

Deficiency codes group by area — the families seen in the Mundra demo
inspection records include: 01 (certificates and documentation), 04 (emergency
systems), 07 (fire safety), 10 (safety of navigation — e.g. charts not
corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners), 11 (life-saving appliances),
13 (propulsion and machinery), 14 (pollution prevention), 18 (labour
conditions / MLC).

Action codes state what must happen, the common ones being: 10 — deficiency
rectified; 15 — rectify at the next port; 16 — rectify within 14 days;
17 — rectify before departure; 30 — grounds for detention. A detainable
deficiency is normally coded 30 with the detention flag

17 — rectify before departure; 30 — grounds for detention. A detainable
deficiency is normally coded 30 with the detention flag set, exactly as the

## Consequences of detention

A detention keeps the ship alongside or at anchor until the recognised
organisation or flag verifies rectification; it raises the ship's and its
flag's risk profile, invites closer targeting across the region, and is a
commercial event (off-hire, delay, reputation). Ports track detention rates as
a fleet-quality indicator — the Sagar Drishti analytics use a PSC detention
benchmark for exactly that purpose, and the vessel watchlist weighs
detentions alongside incidents and findings.

and detention).

# IMO FAL Convention — declarations overview

> Reference summary compiled from public sources for the Sagar Drishti demo
> library. This is a plain-language overview in the library's own words, not
> convention text; consult the FAL Convention and its annex for legal use.

## What the FAL Convention is

The Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic (FAL), 1965,
as amended, is the IMO treaty that simplifies and standardises the paperwork
and formalities around a ship's arrival, stay and departure. Its annex lays
down Standards (binding) and Recommended Practices, built on the principle
that public authorities should not demand more data than necessary, should
accept standard forms, and should not delay the ship.

## The standard FAL declarations

The convention standardises the documents public authorities may require, the
core set being the numbered FAL forms:

1. FAL Form 1 — General Declaration: the master's basic declaration of the
   ship, voyage, arrival/departure particulars and agent.
2. FAL Form 2 — Cargo Declaration: cargo on board, to be loaded or discharged
   (in practice often satisfied by the manifest).
3. FAL Form 3 — Ship's Stores Declaration: stores, bunkers remaining on
   board, and similar consumables.
4. FAL Form 4 — Crew's Effects Declaration: dutiable or restricted personal
   effects of the crew.
5. FAL Form 5 — Crew List: the crew with ranks, nationalities and identity
   documents.
6. FAL Form 6 — Passenger List: passengers where carried.
7. FAL Form 7 — Dangerous Goods: the dangerous goods manifest/declaration
   with IMDG part

   documents.
6. FAL Form 6 — Passenger List: passengers where carried.
7. FAL Form 7 — Dangerous Goods: the dangerous goods manifest/declaration
   with IMDG particulars.

Alongside these, arrival formalities commonly involve the security-related
pre-arrival information under SOLAS XI-2, the Maritime Declaration of Health
under the health regulations, and customs/immigration clearances — the FAL
principle being one submission, standard content, no duplicated demands.

## The single window (2022 amendments)

Amendments adopted in 2022 (in force from 1 January 2024) made the maritime
single window mandatory: public authorities must operate electronic exchange
of the FAL data set for arrival, stay and departure, moving clearance off
paper. The convention also encourages advance submission, 24/7 clearance for
low-risk traffic, and cooperation between authorities so the ship deals with
one interface.

## Shore leave and facilitation

The FAL regime (with the ISPS Code and MLC) supports crew shore leave and
access to shore-based welfare: security measures must be balanced against the
seafarer's need to go ashore — reflected at the demo port by the Gate 3
shore-leave route in ISPS-ADV-02/2026 rather than a denial of leave.

## Local implementation in the demo world

The Mundra demo portal's clearance workflow is a maritime single window in
miniature: Circular CIRC-12/2026 makes electronic lodgement of the FAL 1–7
data mandatory through the port community interface (superseding the interim
CIRC-03/2023 paper/email format), with submission windo

1.1 Bunkering is carried out only by licensed bunker suppliers (licence
register: e.g. Saurashtra Bunkers LLP) with a booking accepted on the port
community interface. Marine Control is informed on VHF Ch 12 before hoses are
connected and after they are disconnected.

1.2 At the outer anchorage, bunker barge operations stand suspended whenever
sea state exceeds 5 or sustained wind exceeds 25 knots (Port Notice
PORT-N-07/2026). Marine Control's broadcast decides; a transfer in progress
when suspension is declared stops, drains and disconnects in a controlled
manner.

1.3 During declared monsoon conditions no new bunker operation starts against
a deteriorating forecast; suppliers shall not push a delivery into a closing
weather window.

## 2. Pre-transfer checklist (ship and barge jointly)

1. Bunker delivery note content agreed — grade, quantity, and a sulphur
   content compliant with MARPOL Annex VI for the fuel's intended use.
2. Mooring of barge alongside checked; fenders in place; safe access rigged.
3. Communications agreed: radio contact

# Mundra SOP MP-04 — Oil spill Tier-1 response SOP

> Demo-world operating procedure authored for the Mundra Port Operations
> Portal / Sagar Drishti demo. Fictional document — not a publication of any
> real port authority.

Document: SOP MP-04 · Owner: HSE & Environment (Chief — HSE) with Marine Department · Status: In force
Applies to: oil spills and sheens within Mundra port limits up to Tier-1 scale
Related: SOP MP-02 (bunkering), MARPOL Annex I overview, incident-management workflow

## 1. Tiered response concept

1.1 Following the IMO tiered-preparedness model: Tier 1 — small operational
spill at or near a facility, handled with port and operator resources (this
SOP); Tier 2 — larger or spreading spill needing regional/mutual-aid
resources; Tier 3 — major spill requiring national response. Under India's
National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (NOS-DCP) the Indian Coast Guard
is the central coordinating agency, so any escalation beyond Tier 1 runs
through the Coast Guard.

1.2 Typical Tier-1 triggers in the demo world: oil sheen at a berth during
bunkering, hose disconnection, ballast operations or sludge transfer; minor
overside leakage from machinery spaces.

## 2. Immediate actions (first 15 minutes)

1. STOP the source: halt the transfer/operation, close valves, plug the leak
   (MP-02 makes the emergency stop signal part of every bunkering).
2. Report: first informer calls Marine Control on VHF Ch 12 (or Ch 16) —
   position/berth, source if known, estimated size and drift. Marine Control
   opens an ENVIRONMENT / OIL_SPILL incident in the portal (severity p

3. Restrict: Marine Control broadcasts to restrict small-craft movement near

4. Muster: the on-scene team (terminal HSE, ship's SOPEP team, harbour

the vessel's manifold area as a precaution; the skimmer is brought to
standby. Tug Samudra Tez (TUG-05) embarks the port's oil-spill kit and is

positioning.

used at the shoreline touch points. Recovered oil and used sorbents go to
sealed drums for disposal through the licensed waste contractor — never back
overside.

3.3 Dispersants are NOT used at Tier 1 in port waters without the explicit
direction of the authorities.

4.1 Water samples are collected for analysis from the slick and a control
point (the portal's evidence pack pattern: water-sample analysis, site
photographs, master's statement via the agent).

4.2 Notifications logged in the communications register:
- Coast Guard Station Okha — informed with reference number (mandatory for
  any escalation

manifests on file, notifications are answered, and the RCA with preventive
actions is approved. Tier-1 performance indicator: boom in the water within
30 minutes of report at any wet berth.
